article.title: AI Isn’t Coming for Our Jobs. It’s Coming for Our Wages.
article.author: Nuno Teles
article.content: The Economist recently ran a cover entitled “ Prepare for an AI jobs apocalypse ,” citing widespread fear among the American public of artificial-intelligence-induced job losses. Such fearmongering is far from new. Information technology breakthroughs have led to many such announcements over the last few decades. In the 1990s, we had the computer scare, prompted by best-selling authors such as Jeremy Rifkin and Viviane Forrester . More recently, in 2013, we had the robot menace, when an Oxford study estimated that 47 percent of jobs in the United States were at risk of computerization. At both times, such prophecies coincided with mass unemployment, not caused by technology but by economic recessions driven by financial instability and austerity policies. Yet such stories helped to naturalize and depoliticize unemployment. Old Stories About New Machines As The Economist points out, the scenario today is different. The predicted mass destruction of jobs coincides, in fact, with historically high employment. Given the ongoing investment boom not only in data center infrastructure but also in upstream utilities such as water and electricity supply, the AI frenzy is now arguably creating more jobs than it is destroying. Another peculiarity is that the current narrative of the job-apocalypse story is driven by AI giants as a marketing strategy to sell their large language models (LLMs) to financial investors and, therefore, feed the ongoing financial euphoria. Nonetheless, the Left should not dismiss the potential systemic effects of AI in the labor process, notably its role in de-skilling and devaluing labor. AI needs to be historically understood and situated as a breakthrough born from concentration and centralization — and of capital’s struggle with labor. The view of technology as a source of mass unemployment is part and parcel of the history of industrial capitalism. In the wake of the Luddite movement at the beginning of the nineteenth century, political economists John McCulloch and David Ricardo debated the effects of introducing new machinery — an argument Karl Marx would later describe as labor compensation theory. In an equilibrium economy where supply creates its own demand, the introduction of a new labor-saving technology in one sector leads to savings and lower prices, which in turn spur new investment. The resulting demand for machinery and products is then expected to create jobs in other sectors: workers are needed to produce the new machinery, while falling prices free income for expenditure on other goods. And, perhaps more significant, lower wages would lead to higher demand for labor. In Volume I of Capital , Marx reconstructs and critiques compensation theory. He dismisses the simple argument that jobs created in machinery production necessarily compensate for the labor displaced by the introduction of machines. Because machinery is only introduced when the labor required to produce it is less than the labor it replaces, its production cannot, by itself, reabsorb all the displaced workers. That is to say, new capital goods cannot theoretically add labor time to the total social labor involved in producing of a commodity. Marx admits that the introduction of new machinery might be accompanied by the creation of social labor across sectors, depending on the length of the workday and the ratios of variable and constant capital. Downstream, the availability of displaced workers might create markets for refined forms of consumption and nonproductive services such as domestic labor as well as, significantly, new public works and infrastructure. Rejecting the assumption of equilibrium in a capitalist economy, Marx points instead to the need for “expanded” capital reproduction, as competition among capitalists drives new investment and the concentration and centralization of capital. In the midst of the current investment frenzy in data centers, transportation, and energy infrastructure, this seems to be the case now with AI. The nexus between capital accumulation, mechanization, and unemployment seems to arise mainly from the urge to substitute variable capital in periods when the industrial reserve army is small and there is a pressing need for the general pauperization of workers. The Specter of Harry Braverman More than the job-destroying effect, Marx’s interest lies in the effects of mechanization and automation on the labor process, including how they extend the working day and de-skill workers. The new industrial machines replaced human force with a natural prime mover — in the form of fossil capital, as Andreas Malm has shown — and replaced “rule of thumb by the conscious application of natural science.” However, these trends did not lighten the burden of labor or make it more socially rewarding. Technological progress is instead driven by the pursuit of surplus value: “Along with the tool, the skill of the worker in handling it passes over to the machine . . . a tendency to equalize and reduce to an identical level every kind of work.” It creates the possibility of longer working hours, the intensification of labor, and the employment of women and children. Marx’s insights were picked up and elaborated upon by Harry Braverman in his famous book Labor and Monopoly Capital . Braverman identifies a progressive de-skilling in the labor process within the context of the widespread application of Taylorist management techniques in the United States. Information technologies, then taking their first steps, were understood as tools that enabled the progressive fragmentation of intellectual labor, facilitating the loss of workers’ control over the labor process and their de-skilling. For Braverman, there was a close relationship between postwar capitalism, characterized by the emergence of large monopolies concentrating capital and labor, the Taylorist management of work, and the technological innovations associated with it. Growing monopoly power in a stagnant demand market, the compression of worker autonomy, and the suppression of the creative dimensions of labor converged in the pursuit of profit at the expense of devaluing wage labor. Braverman’s work was subject to various criticisms . Particularly justified was the criticism of his “monopoly capital” theoretical framework, according to which, monopoly capital would be directed more to de-skilling than to the continued restructuring forced by competition. Braverman’s emphasis on de-skilling didn’t anticipate the new forms of skilled and complex work created by technological information technologies, management techniques, and new labor segments, notably in the financial and telecommunications sectors. Nonetheless, if we consider how relentless capital competition has led to the centralization and concentration of capital — which, in turn, enabled an overall restructuring of capital beginning in the 1970s — Braverman’s arguments gain new relevance. He did not conceive of transformations in the labor process as mechanical or homogeneous but rather as embedded in the specific historical contexts. The De-skilling Machine Par Excellence The introduction of information technologies and logistical innovations transformed the way big multinationals organize production, enabling them to relocate it to new destinations where they could exploit cheap, de-skilled labor, disciplined by still prevailing Taylorist management techniques. The internationalization and restructuring of capital were increasingly centered on new intangible technologies in the form of knowledge and intellectual property, subject to wild financial valuations. Meanwhile, the resurgence of wage labor and exploitation was not limited to the Global South. Eventually, the neoliberal offensive — the growing individualization of labor relations and the introduction, through information technologies, of new forms of competition among workers — created new forms of labor de-skilling, control, and devaluation, as in the case of so-called platform work. Braverman’s attention to the role of technology in supervising and regulating the labor process reinforces Marx’s insight that one of the main drivers for technological innovation in a capitalist economy is the effort to expropriate workers of their specific capacities and knowledge in order to transform them into mere bearers of a homogeneous labor power in commodity production. It comes as no surprise, then, that the AI aims to sell itself as a labor-saving, labor-de-skilling machine. Today the de-skilling and devaluation of labor are explicit goals of the big so-called tech multinationals dedicated to developing large language models. Labor de-skilling is, in fact, embedded in AI technology genesis. As Matteo Pasquinelli shows in his social history of AI, contrary to common wisdom, AI is not the “imitation of biological intelligence” but the imitation of the capitalist division of the labor process. The breakthrough of artificial intelligence centers on its capacity to organize information through feedback loops that “learn” from formidable quantities of internet data, searching for social patterns expressed in language. The spontaneous and adaptive model of LLMs draws its metaphor not so much from solving the enigma of the human brain as from an efficient, decentralized, market-conforming mechanism of information processing. Intelligence becomes the reproduction of patterns adequate to performing layers of simple tasks through a single, apparently conscious and dialogical technology. Apart from the glitches associated with any new technology, such as hallucinations, AI suffers from the more fundamental epistemic problem of understanding knowledge as a reshuffling of given information. It is effective as a powerful processing machine for many “simple” intellectual tasks but is limited to reproducing the conventional knowledge on which it is trained. All Power to the AI Soviets AI is not coming for all our jobs. It will create new ones, as compensation theory suggests. What is more certain is that it is a powerful tool for de-skilling and devaluing intellectual work, making it increasingly homogeneous and mediocre and robbing large segments of both intellectual and manual workers of autonomy in the labor process. As Marx pointed out: “Capitalist production, therefore, only develops the techniques and the degree of combination of the social process of production by simultaneously undermining the original sources of all wealth — the soil and workers.” But AI’s capacity to prey on labor and nature does not mean that the Left should adopt a Luddite position. Unchecked AI will come for our wages through its use as a de-skilling tool. But this technology should be treated as new arena for class struggle in the workplace, where this intangible machine could be used a substitute for boring intellectual tasks, create new jobs, and provide workers with greater autonomy over their time and greater self-realization through labor. As a general-purpose technology that cuts across different industries, AI presents an opportunity for across-the-board mobilization of labor against capital. The urgent need to organize labor around AI labor should be coupled with the political struggle to treat AI as a public utility, as has been argued in these pages by Mathew Huber and Holly Buck . Given its general-purpose applications and large infrastructural needs, there is a strong case for regulating its uses and planning investment in it, just as governments did with essential services, such as water and energy (both of which AI consumes heavily). The technological breakthroughs of running water and electrification infrastructure in nineteenth century, initially largely the domain of private capital, gave rise to public planning, investment, and ownership of these new means of production, which became the bedrock of the extraordinary productivity gains of the twentieth century. Public provision of these utilities on such a scale would have been impossible without the fight of socialist and communist labor movements for wages, employment, and access to essential services. Perhaps the formula today should be: Soviet power plus electrification — and AI.
